analysis.one_liner: Bars the military from buying or selling common household products containing PFAS "forever chemicals."
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Armed Services Committee on August 6, 2021, and died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made "forever chemicals" used in nonstick, waterproof, and stain-resistant products that can build up in the body and may harm health. This bill would have stopped the Department of Defense from buying or selling items containing them — nonstick cookware, food packaging, carpets, furniture, personal care items, dental floss, sunscreen, cleaning products, and certain clothing — on bases, in commissaries, and in military exchanges. It never got a vote and died at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members, military families, and base communities, who buy food, cookware, clothing, and personal care items at commissaries and exchanges; the bill would have removed PFAS-containing versions of those products from those shelves, reducing their exposure to chemicals linked to health risks. Manufacturers of PFAS-free alternatives would gain a market for their products.

how_it_helps.text: It bars DOD from buying covered items — nonstick cookware, food packaging, carpets, personal care items, dental floss, sunscreen, cleaning products, and certain clothing — if they contain PFAS.

It bans the sale of PFAS-containing covered items on DOD property, including commissaries, base exchanges, online exchange shops, and ship's stores, so military families could no longer buy them on base.
It uses a broad chemical definition covering both fully and partially fluorinated compounds, closing a common loophole where 'PFAS-free' labels miss related chemicals.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of PFAS-containing consumer goods, who would lose military procurement and on-base retail sales for those items, and would need to reformulate or substitute products to keep selling them to the military. Consumers might see slightly higher prices or fewer product options for treated goods.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers a long list of household goods, and requiring all of them to be PFAS-free could raise costs or limit product choices for military exchanges, which serve service members and their families.
The one-year effective date would give suppliers limited time to reformulate products and certify them PFAS-free, which suppliers might argue is operationally difficult.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — cutting military families' exposure to PFAS through everyday products sold on base — is real but modest, since the bill covers a defined list of household and personal items rather than all PFAS uses. The cost is a manageable adjustment for suppliers, who already market PFAS-free alternatives. The bill died in committee without any recorded opposition or debate, so its merits were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elissa Slotkin introduced the bill on August 6, 2021, with Rep. Bill Posey as the sole cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Armed Services Committee the same day; the committee never reported it out, and no further action appears in the record.
When the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, the bill expired and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of PFAS-containing consumer products keep their military procurement and on-base retail sales channels untouched; no company had to reformulate or lose sales. Military families living on or near bases continue to buy PFAS-containing cookware, clothing, and personal care items at exchanges and commissaries.

for.name: House Armed Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never took it up

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a party split to show; it had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and died in committee with no recorded votes.

industries.note: The bill would cut off a sales channel — military procurement and on-base retail — for PFAS-containing household goods and the chemicals used to make them. It died, so nothing changed.

industries.industry: Consumer goods makers (cookware, cosmetics, textiles, cleaning products)
industries.note: Suppliers of these goods to military exchanges would have had to reformulate or certify products PFAS-free within a year. Firms already offering PFAS-free lines would gain an edge.

industries.industry: Military exchange systems (AAFES, Navy Exchange, Marine Corps exchanges)
industries.note: Commissaries and exchanges would have had to pull PFAS-containing versions of covered items from shelves and online shops within a year of enactment.
